claims.source: Twining memorandum, 23 Sep 1947 (archived scan); Condon Report Sec. V Ch. 2
claims.text: The memo is dated 23 September 1947, from Lt. Gen. Nathan Twining, Commanding General Air Materiel Command, to Brig. Gen. George Schulgen, subject 'AMC Opinion Concerning "Flying Discs"'.
'The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious.'

claims.source: Condon Report, Section V Chapter 2, quoting the Twining letter
claims.text: The memo directs consideration of the possibility that the objects 'are of domestic origin -- the product of some high security project' not known to Air Force intelligence or to Air Materiel Command.
The memo recommended a priority project, which was directed on 30 December 1947 as Project SIGN.

claims.source: Twining memorandum, 23 Sep 1947, as reproduced in the standard declassified text
claims.text: The memo also records that the lack of physical evidence in the form of crash-recovered exhibits was a constraint on AMC's analysis.

connections.label: Project SIGN
connections.note: The Condon Report states Twining's 23 September 1947 letter directed establishment of a study of UFOs, which received priority designation in December 1947 and began as Project SIGN.

desc: The founding document of the American UFO record. Lt. Gen. Nathan F. Twining, commanding Air Materiel Command, wrote to Brig. Gen. George Schulgen at Air Force intelligence on 23 September 1947 setting out AMC's considered opinion after the summer wave. The memo states that 'the phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious', describes operating characteristics including extreme rates of climb, manoeuvrability and evasive action when detected, and recommends a priority classified project — the recommendation that produced Project SIGN in December 1947. Two features make it more than a curiosity. It is an internal document, written for a general officer, with no public audience and therefore no reason to overstate; and it contains the sentence that has never been satisfactorily explained, directing that consideration be given to the possibility the objects are 'of domestic origin -- the product of some high security project not known to AC/AS-2 or this Command.' The commander of the Air Force's foreign materiel exploitation centre is telling the head of Air Force intelligence requirements that a compartment may exist above them both. Whatever else the memo is, it is contemporaneous evidence that the two-star level in September 1947 regarded a black compartment as a live hypothesis.
